# The Linux you actually need {#sec-linux}

::: {.tldr}
You don't need to become a Linux wizard. You need to move around the filesystem, edit a
file, find things, inspect what your jobs produced, and — crucially — keep work alive when
your connection drops, using `tmux`. This chapter is the minimum, and no more.
:::

If you already live in a terminal, skim the `tmux` section and move on. Everything here is
standard Linux; nothing is ARCC-specific except the paths.

## Moving around

```bash
pwd                 # where am I?
ls -lh              # list files, human-readable sizes
cd /project/cowy-firesurro   # go somewhere
cd                  # go home ($HOME)
cd -                # go back to where you just were
```

Three shortcuts you'll use constantly: `~` is your home directory, `.` is "here", and `..`
is "up one". Tab-completion (press <kbd>Tab</kbd> to finish a half-typed path) will save you
more time than any other single habit.

## Looking at files without opening them

```bash
cat file.txt          # dump a whole (small) file
less big.log          # page through a big file; q to quit, / to search
head -n 20 file       # first 20 lines
tail -n 50 file       # last 50 lines
tail -f slurm-123.out # follow a job's output live as it's written
```

`tail -f` on your job's output file is the classic "is my job doing anything?" move.

## Editing files

`nano` is the friendly choice — arrow keys work, and the shortcuts are listed at the bottom
of the screen (`^O` = save, `^X` = exit).

```bash
nano submit.sh
```

`vim` is everywhere and powerful, but has a learning curve; if you don't already know it,
`nano` is fine for editing a submit script. For anything bigger, edit on your laptop and use
the portal's file browser, VS Code's Remote-SSH, or `rsync` (@sec-moving-data).

## Finding things

```bash
grep -r "account" .          # search file contents recursively
find . -name "*.nc"          # find files by name
find . -size +1G             # find files bigger than 1 GB (great for quota hunts)
du -sh *                     # how big is each thing in this directory?
```

`du -sh * | sort -h` to find what's eating your quota is a habit worth building, given the
50 GB home limit (@sec-storage).

## Environment variables and your shell

Your shell remembers settings in variables. A few you'll meet:

```bash
echo $HOME        # /home/<username>
echo $USER        # your username
echo $SCRATCH     # /gscratch/<username> — your scratch space
echo $PATH        # where the shell looks for commands
```

To make something permanent (say, a handy alias), add it to `~/.bashrc`:

```bash
alias q='squeue --me'          # see just my jobs
alias proj='cd /project/cowy-firesurro'
```

Run `source ~/.bashrc` (or log out and back in) to apply changes.

## `tmux`: don't let a dropped connection kill your work {#sec-tmux}

This is the most important section in the chapter. When you SSH in and start something —
even a legitimate interactive session — **closing your laptop or losing WiFi kills that
shell and everything running in it.** `tmux` fixes this by keeping your session alive *on the
login node* whether or not you're connected.

```bash
tmux new -s work     # start a named session "work"
#   ... do things, launch an interactive job, watch output ...
#   detach with:  Ctrl-b then d
tmux ls              # list your sessions
tmux attach -t work  # reattach later, even from a different computer
```

The workflow that saves people:

1. SSH into the login node.
2. `tmux new -s work`.
3. Inside tmux, do your editing, submit jobs, launch an interactive session (@sec-interactive).
4. Detach (<kbd>Ctrl-b</kbd> then <kbd>d</kbd>) and close your laptop. It all keeps running.
5. Tomorrow, SSH back in and `tmux attach -t work` — exactly where you left off.

::: {.callout-note}
## tmux keeps *login-node* shells alive — batch jobs don't need it
A submitted batch job (`sbatch`, @sec-anatomy) already runs independently of your
connection — you can log out and it keeps going. `tmux` is for the things that live in *your
shell*: interactive sessions, long-running monitoring, an editor you don't want to lose.
:::

## Permissions, briefly

You'll occasionally see `chmod` and permission strings like `-rw-r-----`. The one you'll
actually use is fixing your SSH keys (`chmod 0600 -R ~/.ssh`, from @sec-first-login) and
occasionally making a script executable:

```bash
chmod +x run.sh
```

There is **no `sudo` on the cluster**, ever. You can't install system packages or change
things outside your own directories — and you don't need to. Everything you install goes in
your own space (@sec-conda) or as modules (@sec-modules).

That's the survival kit. On to where your data actually lives.
